title: Serving runtime: ops, architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling & runbooks
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This page consolidates operational and engineering guidance for Redwood Inference's serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling policy, profiling/playbooks, the benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues and runbooks. It is the canonical reference for oncall, SRE, runtime engineers and platform owners.

Goals
- Provide a single, searchable reference for production troubleshooting and performance tuning.
- Describe kernel scheduling design and operational knobs that affect latency/cost tradeoffs.
- Document profiling steps and standardized benchmarks used for releases.
- Include runbooks for the most common incidents and escalation paths.

Ownership and Contacts
- Runtime owners: eng-serving-runtime team (primary: runtime-core).
- Oncall: runtime-oncall rota (PagerDuty: #runtime-oncall).
- Slack channels: #runtime-ops, #runtime-dev, #perf-analysis.
- Primary stakeholders: product (model-serving), eng-sre (capacity and SLOs).

1) Runtime architecture (high level)

Summary
The runtime implements a multi-tenant, GPU-optimized inference engine with a control plane for routing, scheduling and lifecycle management. Key goals: predictable tail-latency (p99/p999), efficient GPU utilization, and graceful degradation under capacity pressure.

Core components
- API Gateway (rest/gRPC): ingress, auth, rate limiting, per-tenant quotas.
- Router: policy engine that selects model variant (precision, quantization) and target pool (hosted/dedicated/private) based on policy and health.
- Frontend workers: lightweight request preprocessors that perform tokenization and KV-cache lookup.
- Batching service: coalesces compatible requests into generation batches (configurable max_batch_size, max_latency_ms).
- Model workers (per-GPU): host loaded model shards or full-model instances. Expose local IPC to the batching service.
- Kernel scheduler: orchestrates kernel launches across CUDA streams and handles preemption and cooperative scheduling for multi-model multiplexing.
- KV cache service: shared cache for prefix caching and next-token acceleration. Eviction policy LRU with size per-model.
- Metrics/tracing and control plane: Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, and a control plane that handles rollouts and fallback logic.

SLOs (global defaults)
| SLO | Target | Measurement | Owner |
|-----|--------|-------------|-------|
| p50 latency (text-gen) | <= 20 ms/token | rolling 5m | runtime-core |
| p95 latency (text-gen) | <= 80 ms/token | rolling 5m | runtime-core |
| p99 latency (text-gen) | <= 250 ms/token | rolling 5m | eng-sre |
| Availability | 99.95% | monthly | infra |

Operational knobs
- batching.max_batch_size (default: 64)
- batching.max_queue_time_ms (default: 12)
- scheduler.preemption_enabled (true/false)
- kernel.allow_oversubscribe (percentage, default: 10%)
- worker.kv_cache_size_mb (per-model)

2) Kernel scheduling design

Principles
- Minimize head-of-line blocking by combining batching with cooperative preemption.
- Prefer prioritized fairness: latency-sensitive low-token-rate requests are prioritized over long streaming generations when configured.
- Allow controlled oversubscription to increase GPU utilization while keeping tail latency within SLO.

Key mechanisms
- CUDA stream pools: each model worker maintains multiple stream pools (fast/latency vs throughput). The scheduler assigns kernels to streams based on request priority.
- Cooperative kernel yields: long-running kernels (e.g., large-seq decoding loops) periodically check for higher-priority work and yield after N tokens (configurable).
- Time-slicing preemption: for aggressive SLOs, the scheduler will preempt throughput kernels at 200ms boundaries and reschedule.
- Affinity and topology-aware placement: the scheduler prefers colocating model shards with low inter-GPU NVLink latencies.

Scheduling policies (config examples)
- policy: latency-first
  - preemption_enabled: true
  - throughput_weight: 0.2
  - latency_weight: 0.8
- policy: throughput-first
  - preemption_enabled: false
  - throughput_weight: 0.9
  - latency_weight: 0.1

Tuning guidance
- If p99 spikes with low GPU utilization: increase kernel.allow_oversubscribe to 15% and reduce batching.max_queue_time_ms to 8ms.
- If OOMs occur on 80% of runs: reduce worker.model_instances_per_gpu and lower kv_cache_size_mb.

3) Profiling playbook

When to profile
- New model onboarding or new kernel release
- Repeated regressions in p95/p99 latency post-deploy
- Benchmark discrepancies between CI and canary runs

Tools and artifacts
- perf-runner (internal): standardized harness to run microbenchmarks and system-level tests.
- nvprof / Nsight Systems: GPU-level tracing for kernels and memcpy
- BPF/eBPF tracers: observe syscalls and scheduling in host kernel
- Flamegraphs: aggregated kernel+CPU stacks.

Standard profiling procedure (quick playbook)
1. Reproduce a representative workload with perf-runner: ./tools/perf-runner --profile --model resnet-llm --seq-len 1024 --concurrency 8 --duration 300
2. Capture GPU traces: nsys profile -o /tmp/trace --trace=cuda,osrt --stats=true --force-overwrite --output=/tmp/nsys.qdrep -- ./bin/worker --test-run
3. Generate flamegraphs: ./scripts/convert-nsys-to-flame /tmp/nsys.qdrep > /tmp/flame.svg
4. Capture system-level metrics (host): sudo /usr/local/bin/ebpf-trace --out /tmp/host.ebpf
5. Collect NVTX ranges from the worker logs; correlate with flamegraphs.

Common signals to look for
- Long memcpy times -> PCIe bottleneck or host->device transfers not pinned.
- High kernel launch overhead -> context-switching or too many small kernels (work to consolidate kernels or enable fused ops).
- Periodic latency spikes aligned with GC-like events in runtime -> investigate memory allocator or cache eviction.

4) Benchmarking suite

Overview
The benchmarking suite measures end-to-end generation throughput, per-token latency distributions, memory usage, and cost-per-token estimations across representative workloads. Benchmarks are deterministic and versioned.

Workloads included
- small-chat: simulates short-turn chat with seq_len=128, bursty arrivals, low concurrency
- long-gen: seq_len=2048, sustained streaming, medium concurrency
- embedding-bulk: batchable embedding generation for 512-d models

How to run
- CI: ./ci/run_benchmarks.sh --suite=canary --models="gptx-3b,redwood-mini"
- Local: ./tools/bench-run --config benchmarks/canary.yaml --out /tmp/bench.json

Example benchmark config (benchmarks/canary.yaml)

```yaml
suite: canary
workloads:
  - name: small-chat
    seq_len: 128
    concurrency: 16
    duration_seconds: 300
  - name: long-gen
    seq_len: 2048
    concurrency: 8
    duration_seconds: 600
metrics:
  - p50
  - p95
  - p99
  - throughput
  - gpu_utilization
```

Acceptance criteria for release
- p99 for small-chat must not regress more than 10% vs baseline.
- throughput delta < 7% vs baseline for long-gen.
- no new OOM regressions observed over 10 consecutive runs.

5) Release notes (recent)

2029-11-30 — Release v2029.11.30
- Improved kernel fusion for causal attention -> avg token latency -9% for large seq lengths.
- New scheduler: time-slicing preemption enabled by default in latency-first policy.
- Added perf-runner integration with Nsight pipeline.
- Fixed race condition in KV cache eviction that could lead to duplicated cache entries (issue: RUNTIME-3821).

Impact: Can expect improved p95/p99 on long-seq workloads. Follow the profiling playbook after upgrade to validate on your canary fleets.

6) Known issues (selected)
- RUNTIME-4098: Intermittent p99 spikes under mixed workloads when kernel.allow_oversubscribe is > 20%.
  - Mitigation: set kernel.allow_oversubscribe=10% and redeploy. Permanent fix targeted for v2029.12.x.
- RUNTIME-4012: Nsight reports misleading memcpy timings on hosts with Spectre mitigations enabled.
  - Mitigation: run with msr interface disabled or use perf-runner with --skip-nsight.
- RUNTIME-3950: Degenerate tokenization for some non-UTF8 inputs leads to larger-than-expected sequences and OOMs.
  - Mitigation: enforce server-side max_input_chars and normalize inputs at the gateway.

7) Runtime runbooks (playbooks)

A. High p99 latency for text generation
1. Confirm scope: check if issue is single tenant, model, or fleet-wide via /dashboards/runtime/latency
2. Check recent deploys (control plane) and model rollouts (last 30 minutes).
3. Verify GPU utilization: if utilization < 30% and p99 high -> possible scheduling/preemption misconfig.
4. Check batching queue length and max_queue_time_ms. If queue_time > 50ms, lower max_batch_size or tune batching.max_queue_time_ms.
5. Collect traces: run perf-runner profile against a canary instance to reproduce.
6. Escalation: if not resolved in 20 minutes, notify runtime-core oncall and open incident with priority P1. Add SLO impact and affected tenants.

B. OOM on worker process
1. Identify model and worker via logs (/var/log/runtime/worker-*.log). Look for OOM stack traces.
2. Check worker config: model_instances_per_gpu, kv_cache_size_mb.
3. If OOM correlated with increased seq_len, set temporary per-tenant max_seq_len and restart worker.
4. If persistent: drain affected worker, redeploy with reduced instances_per_gpu, and run benchmark to validate.

C. Model quality regression (serving mismatch vs eval)
1. Confirm model binary version and quantization profile in control plane.
2. Run deterministic eval harness in eval-runner against the same model commit.
3. If regression confirmed, rollback to previous model variant and open a regression ticket with perf and eval artifacts.

D. Node-level GPU errors (ECC / hardware faults)
1. Check node health: /tools/node-health --node <node>
2. If ECC errors > threshold (5/hr), cordon the node and escalate to infra-hardware.
3. Replace or retest node in maintenance.

- Run perf-runner locally: ./tools/perf-runner --model redwood-mini --seq-len 512 --concurrency 4 --duration 120
- Dump metrics for last 30m: curl "http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query?query=rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_count[30m])"
